claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi contains partial short-range order or incipient Ti-centered clustering in its nominally simple solid-solution state.
Ti-centered short-range order or clustering reduces the friction stress and activation barriers for dislocation glide.
The reduced resistance to dislocation glide lowers the hardness and strength of CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed short-range order enables easy slip and sustains ductility and machinability.
Strongly B2-ordered structures can have high antiphase-boundary energy that inhibits ordinary dislocation behavior.
Long-range-ordered or more compositionally complex Ti-containing high-entropy alloys exhibit more pronounced hardening than the proposed CoCrFeNiTi state.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy can be treated as a single-phase FCC solid solution with minimal second-phase precipitates.
Partial ordering mitigates the high antiphase-boundary energies associated with strongly ordered structures.
Nanoscopic regions of partial order facilitate cross-slip and thermally activated dislocation motion.
The ordering-assisted dislocation processes occur before long-range order or secondary phases form.
Chemical inhomogeneity or chemical order can alter dislocation-mediated deformation and the strength-ductility balance.
During deformation, local atomic-order changes will be detectable concurrently with dislocation motion in CoCrFeNiTi.
CoCrFeNiTi will show a modest increase in latent hardening relative to an ideal random solid solution.
The proposed mechanism is primarily applicable to near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi below approximately 600 °C.
Substantial composition changes or extended high-temperature exposure can promote second-phase precipitation that obscures the proposed mechanism.
A CoCrFeNi reference lacking Ti is a purely random solid solution suitable for isolating the effect of Ti-centered ordering.
Absence of measurable short-range order or clustering would falsify an SRO-mediated explanation.
Failure of local ordering to change under load would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The proposed mechanism can operate through pre-existing, static short-range order that facilitates dislocation motion, but the falsification rule treats failure of ordering to change under load as disproof. Static but mechanically active SRO would satisfy the mechanism while failing this criterion.
